item.title: Demystifying phone unlocking tools: A technical overview
item.description:
This post is a written description of a presentation titled Phone unlocking tools and where to find them that we have delivered privately to different events and organizations, including Primavera Hacker 25, the Freedom of the Press Foundation, and the Public Interest Technology Group. It provides a technical overview of how commercial forensic tools compromise mobile devices, focusing on the specific attack surfaces exploited at each stage of the device lifecycle. Further posts will focus on sample analysis, and defenses. See also the previous posts of this serie:

Introduction #

Commercial phone unlocking tools are not magic. They exploit the same classes of vulnerabilities that security researchers publish about at conferences and in academic papers. What makes them distinctive is not the novelty of the techniques, but the systematic commercialization of exploitation: acquiring or developing exploits for each hardware and software combination, and reaching a certain degree of stability, packaging them into automated workflows that require minimal operator expertise.

This post aims to demystify the technical foundations of these tools. The attack vectors available to a forensic examiner with physical access to a device are constrained by well-understood boundaries: the boot chain, the trusted execution environment, the secure element (when present), and the kernel’s peripheral driver stack. This post mostly details Android internals, however iOS equivalent concepts are technically similar.

Much of the background research referenced here comes from Quarkslab, whose extensive publications on TEEs, and Android’s data encryption architecture have been invaluable to understand these tools. Their work, alongside reporting from Amnesty International’s Security Lab and other NGOs, and analysis by the GrapheneOS project, provides the empirical basis for the claims made in this post.

Hardware security architecture #

Before examining attack vectors, it is necessary to understand the hardware security architecture of modern Android devices. The following sections describe the components that forensic tools must eventually hack or bypass.

The System-on-Chip: Normal World and Secure World #

Modern ARM-based mobile processors implement TrustZone, a hardware security extension that partitions the processor into two execution environments: the Normal World and the Secure World. The Normal World runs the Android operating system, user applications, and the Linux kernel. The Secure World runs a separate, minimal operating system, the Trusted OS, along with small, specialized applications known as Trusted Applications (TAs).

The two worlds share the same physical processor cores but are hardware-isolated: the Normal World cannot directly read or write Secure World memory. Communication between the two happens through a monitor, a piece of code running at the highest privilege level (EL3 on ARMv8), which handles context switches triggered by Secure Monitor Call (SMC) instructions. Each physical processor core effectively provides two virtual cores, with the Non-Secure bit in the Secure Configuration Register determining which world is active at any given time.

The Trusted OS hosts critical security services. Two are directly relevant to device unlocking:

Gatekeeper: responsible for verifying user credentials (PIN, password, pattern). It implements rate-limiting to throttle brute-force attempts and, upon successful authentication, issues a signed authentication token. Keymaster: the key management service that stores and operates on cryptographic keys. Some keys are authentication-bound, meaning they can only be used after Gatekeeper has issued a valid token.

Different SoC vendors ship different TrustZone implementations. Google (and AOSP in general) uses TrustyOS; Qualcomm uses QSEE; Samsung uses TEEGRIS (on both Exynos and MediaTek SoCs in Samsung devices); Huawei uses TrustedCore; Trustonic’s Kinibi is also often found on MediaTek and Exynos SoCs. The security properties vary between implementations.

The Secure Element #

A Secure Element (SE) is a physically separate, tamper-resistant hardware chip that provides an additional layer of security beyond the TEE. Unlike the Secure World, which runs on the same SoC as the Normal World, a Secure Element is an independent processor with its own boot chain, its own firmware, and its own cryptographic key storage.

In the Android ecosystem, the Secure Element is exposed through the StrongBox API (introduced in Android 9). Google’s Pixel phones, starting with the Pixel 3, include the Titan M chip as their Secure Element, that was later upgraded with the Titan M2 from Pixel 6 onward. On Apple devices, the equivalent is the Secure Enclave Processor (SEP).

The Secure Element’s role in device encryption is to hold key-encryption keys and enforce rate-limiting for credential verification in hardware that the main SoC cannot tamper with, even if fully compromised. This is an important distinction: on a device without a Secure Element, compromising the TEE is sufficient to extract or bypass credential-derived keys. On a device with a Secure Element, the attacker must additionally compromise a separate, hardened chip.

Unfortunately, only flagship devices typically include a Secure Element. Most mid-range and budget devices rely solely on the TEE for credential protection. This architectural gap is the single most important factor determining the chances that a device has to resist forensic unlocking when powered off.

The boot chain #

The boot chain establishes a chain of trust from immutable hardware to the running operating system. Each stage verifies the integrity of the next before executing it.

The chain proceeds as follows:

Boot ROM: the first code executed at power-on. It is burned into silicon at manufacture and is, in principle, immutable and unpatchable (with a few modern exceptions to deploy patches for vulnerabilities). The Boot ROM verifies and loads the next stage (the preloader or secondary bootloader). It forms the hardware root of trust.

Preloader/Secondary Bootloader (BL2): loaded and verified by the Boot ROM. On MediaTek SoCs, this is often called the preloader. It initializes hardware, loads the Trusted OS into the Secure World, and loads the main bootloader into the Normal World.

Trusted OS: loaded into the Secure World by the preloader. It hosts Gatekeeper, Keymaster, and other Trusted Applications. Its integrity is verified by the preloader as part of the secure boot chain.

Bootloader (BL3): the Normal World bootloader (e.g., Little Kernel on MediaTek, ABL on Qualcomm). It enforces Android Verified Boot (AVB), anti-rollback protections, and device-state checks before loading the Android kernel.

Android OS: the Linux kernel and userspace. Verified Boot (dm-verity) ensures the integrity of system partitions at runtime.

When a Secure Element is present, it runs its own independent boot chain in parallel: Boot ROM â Bootrom EXT â Bootloader â OS. The Secure Element’s boot chain is entirely separate from the SoC’s, providing the most isolation.

If any stage in the boot chain is compromised, all subsequent stages are untrustworthy. This is why Boot ROM vulnerabilities are so devastating: they are often unpatchable, they undermine everything built on top, and they affect every device using the vulnerable silicon for its entire hardware lifetime.

Android data encryption #

Understanding the attack vectors requires understanding what the attacker is ultimately trying to obtain: the decryption keys for the user’s data.

Full Disk Encryption vs. File-Based Encryption #

Android has used two encryption schemes over its history:

Full Disk Encryption (FDE) encrypts the entire data partition with a single key, derived from the user’s credentials. The key must be available before the OS can boot, so the user is prompted for their PIN or password at boot time. FDE was the default until Android 6 and has been deprecated since Android 13.

File-Based Encryption (FBE) encrypts individual files with different keys, allowing more granular access control. FBE has been the default since Android 7 and is required since Android 10. It divides storage into two classes:

Device Encrypted (DE) storage: available immediately after boot, before the user authenticates. Used for system-critical functionality (alarms, phone dialer, Direct Boot). The DE key is derived without user credentials. Credential Encrypted (CE) storage: available only after the user authenticates for the first time after boot. This is where all user data residesâmessages, photos, application data. The CE key is derived from the user’s credentials, stretched through scrypt, and protected by keys held in the TEE (and, when present, the Secure Element). CE key derivation: The role of credentials #

Quarkslab’s Android Data Encryption in depth provides the most detailed public analysis of how the CE key is derived. The process, in simplified form, proceeds as follows:

The user’s credentials (PIN, password, or pattern) are stretched using scrypt, a memory-hard key derivation function, with parameters and salt stored in DE-protected files under /data/system_de/<uid>/spblob. The scrypt step is intentionally slow: it introduces a negligible delay for a single authentication attempt but makes brute-forcing computationally expensive.

The stretched credentials are combined with other material to form a password blob, which is sent to the Gatekeeper Trusted Application in the TEE. Gatekeeper verifies the blob against a stored password handle using an HMAC with an internal key. If verification succeeds, Gatekeeper issues a signed authentication token.

The authentication token is presented to Keymaster, which uses it to unlock an authentication-bound key. This key is used to perform the first decryption of the Synthetic Password, an intermediate secret stored in encrypted form on the filesystem.

The Synthetic Password is decrypted a second time using a key derived from the user’s credentials (the applicationId). This second decryption uses AES-GCM, which provides authenticated encryption: if the wrong credentials are supplied, the GCM tag will not match and decryption will fail. This is the cryptographic check that ultimately binds the CE key to the correct credentials.

From the Synthetic Password, the system derives the CE file encryption keys used by the Linux kernel’s fscrypt subsystem to decrypt individual files.

The critical observation is that user credentials are cryptographically embedded in the key derivation chain. There is no way to bypass them purely through software attacks: an attacker who compromises the TEE can bypass the authentication token check, but they still need to brute-force the credentials through scrypt to derive the correct key material.

Key derivation with a Secure Element (Weaver) #

On devices with a Secure Element, the key derivation process includes an additional step. Instead of relying solely on Gatekeeper in the TEE, the system uses Weaver, a service running on the Secure Element. Weaver stores a secret value that is released only upon correct credential verification and enforces its own independent rate-limiting.

This means that even if an attacker fully compromises the TEE, or other Trusted Applications as shown by Synacktiv’s Kinibi TEE blogpost, they cannot extract the Weaver secret or bypass its throttling, if implemented properly. Brute-forcing must proceed online, at the rate the Secure Element permits, which, for a device like the Pixel with Titan M, means exponential backoff.

Attack vectors #

With the architecture established, we can now map the specific attack surfaces that forensic tools exploit. These fall into two main categories, corresponding to teo device states: powered off or powered on but never unlocked (BFU), and powered on and previously unlocked (AFU).

BFU attacks on devices without a Secure Element #

The most complete form of BFU attack targets the boot chain itself. If an attacker can compromise the Boot ROM or the preloader, they can break the entire chain of trust, including the TEE.

The attack proceeds as follows:

Boot ROM exploitation: the attacker connects to the device via USB and exploits a vulnerability in the Boot ROM (or uses a vendor-specific download/recovery mode, such as MediaTek’s Download Mode or Qualcomm’s EDL mode) to gain code execution before the bootloader runs.

Boot chain patching: with Boot ROM-level access, the attacker patches or replaces the preloader to disable secure boot verification of subsequent stages. This allows loading a modified Trusted OS and modified Trusted Applications.

TEE patching: the attacker replaces or patches Gatekeeper to accept any credentials and issue valid authentication tokens regardless of input. They also patch or extract keys from Keymaster. As Quarkslab demonstrated in their proof-of-concept on Samsung A22 devices (MT6769V and MT6833V SoCs), this involved patching Samsung’s TEEGRIS operating system: first disabling verification of the root filesystem, then disabling TA signature verification, and finally patching Gatekeeper’s credential comparison to always succeed.

Key material extraction: with a rooted Android system and a compromised TEE, the attacker extracts the encrypted Synthetic Password and the intermediate decryption result from Keymaster.

Offline brute force: the attacker now has all the material needed for offline brute-forcing. The brute-force loop is:

Generate a candidate password Stretch it through scrypt with the stored parameters Derive the applicationId Attempt AES-GCM decryption of the Synthetic Password If the GCM tag matches, the correct credentials have been found

Because this brute-force runs entirely offline, on the attacker’s hardware, it is bounded only by computational resources and password complexity. A numeric PIN of six digits or fewer is trivially recoverable. Even longer numeric PINs fall quickly on dedicated hardware. Only a strong alphanumeric and symbols password provides meaningful resistance.

MediaTek devices are particularly vulnerable to this attack. Multiple MediaTek SoCs contain Boot ROM vulnerabilities that are publicly known and exploited by open-source tools such as MTKClient. Because Boot ROM code is immutable, these vulnerabilities cannot be patched: every device using the affected silicon is permanently compromised, regardless of Android version or security patch level. Quarkslab’s proof-of-concept targeted exactly this class of device, demonstrating the full chain from Boot ROM exploit to CE key recovery.

BFU attacks on devices with a Secure Element #

When a Secure Element is present, the attack chain is fundamentally harder. Even if the attacker achieves everything described above, they still cannot extract the Weaver secret from the Secure Element, under normal circumstances. Chances of a Secure Element exploit are pretty low, especially as being distributed as part of a widely available forensics commercial suite.

As anticipated, the Secure Element runs its own independent boot chain on physically separate silicon. Its keys cannot be extracted by the main SoC, and its rate-limiting logic is enforced in hardware that the attacker does not control.

The result is that brute-force can often only proceed online: each attempt must query the Secure Element, which enforces some kind of backoff. This slows down the attack significantly. A ten-digit PIN that falls in seconds to offline brute-force may take a long time against a properly implemented Secure Element. An alphanumeric password becomes likely unbreakable.

This is why, according to Cellebrite’s own February 2025 support matrix, brute-force capabilities are generally not available for Pixel devices with Titan M. The Secure Element is doing exactly what it was designed to do.

That said, the Secure Element is not immune to vulnerabilities. Quarkslab demonstrated code execution on the Titan M chip through CVE-2022-20233, a single-byte out-of-bounds write in the Keymaster task that could be exploited to hijack execution flow. This vulnerability has since been patched, but it demonstrates that Secure Elements, while vastly more resistant than TEE-only configurations, can still have issues. Google is offering up to $1,500,000 for a zero-click vulnerabilities on the Pixel Titan M2.

AFU attacks: The lock screen is just UI #

After the first unlock, the threat model fully changes. In AFU state, the CE decryption keys are loaded in memory and remain there. The lock screen is no longer a cryptographic barrier, it is just a user interface element, a screen overlay that prevents interaction but does not re-encrypt data.

This means that an AFU attacker does not need to brute-force credentials at all. They need to achieve code execution in the kernel or a privileged process, at which point they have direct access to the decrypted filesystem. The lock screen is bypassed, and no encryption needs to be broken.

The primary attack surface in AFU state is the USB interface. When a device is locked but in AFU state, the USB controller remains active and exposes the device’s kernel to a substantial attack surface.

As the diagram illustrates, a peripheral emulator connected to a locked device’s USB port can interact with the kernel through approximately 200 reachable drivers, including MTP (Media Transfer Protocol), MSC (Mass Storage Class), HID (Human Interface Device), Audio, and CVC (Communication Voice Class) subsystems. Each of these drivers is a potential attack surface for memory corruption vulnerabilities.

The exploit used by Cellebrite against a Serbian activist’s device in December 2024, as documented by Amnesty International, attempted to use at least three Linux kernel USB driver vulnerabilities:

CVE-2024-53104: a vulnerability in the USB Video Class (UVC) driver. CVE-2024-53197: an out-of-bounds write in the ALSA USB-audio driver, triggered when a malicious USB device provides a bNumConfigurations value exceeding allocated memory. This vulnerability affects legacy code present since Linux kernel 2.6.26 (2008) and was confirmed by CISA to be actively exploited in the wild. CVE-2024-50302: a memory leak in the HID subsystem that exposes uninitialized kernel memory, including encryption keys and authentication tokens, when processing crafted USB HID reports.

The Cellebrite Turbo Link device, a specialized hardware adapter that connects between the forensic workstation and the target device, likely functions as a peripheral emulator capable of presenting itself as multiple USB device types in rapid succession, probing for each vulnerability to achieve kernel-level code execution.

Many of these USB drivers are loaded by default and remain reachable even when the device is locked. The kernel does not distinguish between a legitimate USB accessory and a malicious peripheral emulator, thus this is the main weakness that AFU exploitation often relies upon.

AFU attacks on locked devices in practice #

Once the attacker achieves kernel code execution through USB driver exploitation, the lock screen is irrelevant. The attacker can:

Directly read the decrypted filesystem, since CE keys are already in memory Perform a Full File System (FFS) extraction of all user data Access application data, messages, photos, credentials, and metadata Potentially install persistent backdoors

As we already knew, a device in AFU state is fundamentally less secure than a device in BFU state, regardless of the strength of the user’s password or the presence of a Secure Element. The Secure Element protects credential-derived keys at boot; it does not protect already-decrypted data in memory after the first unlock.

This is confirmed by Cellebrite’s February 2025 support matrix, which shows AFU extraction capabilities even for devices (including recent Pixels with stock Android) that resist BFU attacks. Notably, according to the same documentation, GrapheneOS on Pixel devices resists AFU extraction, probably thanks to the attack surface reduction and the USB restrictions that are implemented beyond stock Android.

A note on iOS: checkm8 and USB Restricted Mode #

Apple devices face analogous attack surfaces. The checkm8 exploit, publicly released in 2019, targets an unpatchable Boot ROM vulnerability present in all Apple devices from the iPhone 4S through the iPhone X (A5 through A11 SoCs). Like MediaTek Boot ROM vulnerabilities, checkm8 cannot be fixed through software updates: every affected device is permanently exploitable.

For newer Apple devices, AFU attacks rely on USB-based exploitation. Apple introduced USB Restricted Mode in iOS 11.4.1 to mitigate this: if the device has been locked for more than one hour, the Lightning or USB-C port is restricted to charging only, disabling data connections that forensic tools require.

However, Quarkslab’s analysis of CVE-2025-24200 (reported by CitizenLab) revealed that USB Restricted Mode was bypassable. The vulnerability, reported by Citizen Lab and patched in iOS 18.3.1, allowed a physical attacker to re-enable USB data connections on a locked device by exploiting a flaw in the Accessibility framework. The profiled daemon, which handles device management settings, failed to check whether the device was locked before processing requests to disable USB Restricted Mode. In other words, the USB port was only soft-disabled: something as simple as a logic bug in the policy enforcement allowed it to be re-enabled.

Forensic vendors have already started producing countermeasures to Apple’s inactivity reboot. Cellebrite’s Spring 2026 release for Inseyets advertises a “Safeguard Mode” that “mitigates the impact of iOS inactivity reboot timers by preserving access to a device” â in practice, preventing the device from returning to BFU state once they have AFU access. Magnet Forensics ships a hardware product called GrayKey Preserve which similarly aims to suppress the auto-reboot, network wipes and remote wipes on captured devices. These tools likely ship the same AFU exploits in a different, locked-down chassis that performs only preservation rather than extraction, which is also why they can move faster than the full extraction suites.

Defensive implications #

The attack vectors described above lead to a clear set of defensive priorities.

BFU is your best defense #

The most impactful single action when facing potential device seizure is to power the device off. This returns it to BFU state, where:

CE storage is encrypted and keys are not in memory USB driver exploitation cannot yield decrypted data The attacker must compromise the boot chain and brute-force credentials On devices with a Secure Element, brute-force is rate-limited by hardware Enable Lockdown Mode on iOS #

iOS users should enable Lockdown Mode. It hardens the device against exploitation across messaging, web, and attachments, and there is public-record evidence of it stopping at least one extraction attempt: an FBI CART court filing on an iPhone 13 explicitly states that “Because the iPhone was in Lockdown mode, CART could not extract that device”. The mechanism is not officially documented, but it is consistent with what Lockdown Mode is known to do: shrink the reachable attack surface, restrict USB more aggressively, and block the configuration-profile and MDM enrollment that forensic and “jailbreak” tools have historically abused to sideload unverified components.

Auto-reboot: returning to BFU automatically #

If a device cannot be manually powered off, an automatic reboot mechanism provides the next best defense. After a configurable period without user authentication, the device reboots, returning to BFU state and purging decryption keys from memory.

GrapheneOS has implemented this feature for years. Apple introduced it in iOS 18. Stock Android on Pixel devices gained a limited version in Android 15, but its implementation remains less configurable and less aggressive than GrapheneOS’s. The feature is the most useful if the timeout is short (2-4 hours) and loses its value when its multiple days, as Google enforces likely as a result of negotiation with law enforcement. GrapheneOS in particular allows the timeout to be configured very low, precisely because the team has long considered the risk of an exploit being produced to inhibit the reboot itself.

USB port restriction #

Disabling USB data transfer when the device is locked directly eliminates the AFU attack surface described above. Android 15 introduces USB restriction options; iOS has had USB Restricted Mode since version 11. GrapheneOS provides more trustworthy and configurable USB restriction.

Password strength #

The brute-force analysis makes the case for strong passwords unambiguous:

A 4-digit PIN: trivially crackable offline, and crackable even online within hours to days A 6-digit PIN: trivially crackable offline; crackable online within days to weeks depending on rate-limiting implementation A pattern: equivalent to or weaker than a short PIN in entropy An alphanumeric password of 10+ characters with mixed case and symbols: computationally unlikely to brute-force offline through scrypt; almost impossible to brute-force online against a Secure Element

The password is only required at boot. Biometric authentication (fingerprint, face recognition) handles daily unlocking, unless the user is in a jurisdiction where physical coercion is likely, whether lawfully or not. The marginal inconvenience of entering a strong password once after each reboot is minimal compared to the protection it provides.

Device choice #

According to Cellebrite’s own February 2025 documentation:

MediaTek-based devices: effectively no mitigation possible against BFU attacks due to unpatchable Boot ROM vulnerabilities. Most non-Pixel, non-Samsung Android devices: considered unlockable, with few exceptions, due to a combination of delayed security updates, weak TEE implementations, and absent Secure Elements. Samsung devices (Exynos): partial protection, varying by model and patch level. Google Pixel with stock Android: resistant to BFU attacks on recent models, but AFU file system extraction is possible. Google Pixel with GrapheneOS: resistant to both BFU and AFU attacks on recent models (6a and newer). This is the strongest protection available on any Android device.

A subsequent Cellebrite matrix leaked in October 2025 suggests Cellebrite has since also lost Full File System extraction support against unlocked GrapheneOS devices.

It is worth noting that alternative Android distributions such as LineageOS or CalyxOS, while valuable for other reasons, do not meaningfully change the forensic unlocking picture from the stock or vendor ROM.

Application-level encryption #

Applications that implement their own encryption layer with a separate password can provide defense-in-depth against full device compromise. Password managers’ master password vaults are a good example: even if the entire device filesystem is extracted, the vault remains encrypted under a key that the forensic tool has not obtained.

However, the effectiveness of application-level protection depends on several factors: whether the app actually implements its own encryption independently from the OS credential protection, whether decryption keys remain in memory after first unlock (making them vulnerable to AFU extraction), whether the app relies on the system biometric authentication (which, without a Secure Element, is broken along with the rest of the OS key hierarchy), and whether notifications or message previews are cached in plaintext outside the app’s encrypted storage.

Conclusion #

The way these tools operate is not magic nor secret. The more we collect samples, reverse engineer and read promotional and support material, the better we understand capabilities and defenses.

As we said many times these tools simply shouldn’t commercially exist. The companies that build these tools are active participants in the zero-day vulnerability trade, stockpiling security flaws that weaken every device, for every user, everywhere. The technical defenses described here are effective but place the burden on individuals and communities.

Update (20 May 2026): following feedback from Final of the GrapheneOS Foundation, this post was updated with information about iOS Lockdown Mode, forensic-vendor countermeasures to iOS inactivity reboot (Cellebrite Safeguard Mode and Magnet GrayKey Preserve), GrapheneOS’s auto-reboot design rationale, and the October 2025 Cellebrite matrix leak.

No Flax, no Equinox, no PyTorch. Params are plain dicts of arrays and every part of the model is a function you can read top to bottom in deepseek_v3.py.

Read the write-up: DeepSeek V3 in 190 lines of pure JAX, with diagrams, the code explained piece by piece, and the results.

Idea from the paper What it does Where Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) Caches one small latent per token instead of full keys and values: 480 → 144 numbers per token per layer here mla, init_cache Decoupled RoPE One rotary key shared by all heads, kept outside the compressed latent rope, apply_rope, mla DeepSeekMoE 1 shared expert that always runs + 16 routed experts, top-4 per token route, moe Auxiliary-loss-free balancing A per-expert bias nudges routing toward idle experts; it changes which experts are picked, not their weights update_bias, route Sequence-wise balance loss The small complementary loss from the paper (α = 1e-4) seq_balance_loss Multi-token prediction (MTP) An extra module also predicts the token after next, weighted λ = 0.3 in the loss forward, loss_fn Training and generation bf16 compute on f32 master weights; prefill + decode with the MLA cache make_train_step, generate

One run of the default config on a MacBook Air M5 (24 GB):

Model 36.2M parameters, 13.6M active per token Data 207 books, 21.7M training tokens (Hammett repeated 3×); validation is held-out crime fiction Training 12,000 steps, ~98M tokens (~4.5 epochs), ~2.6 h Speed ~10.7k tokens/s (median) Validation loss 5.02 (step 250) → 3.51 Expert load, with bias 5.7–6.9% per expert (even is 6.25%), at step 2000 Expert load, without bias 0.09–18.6% per expert, at step 2000

With balancing on and off, validation loss at step 2000 was the same (3.921 vs 3.923). The bias evens out the experts without costing anything, which is the paper's claim.

Its own words, from the prompt "The fog came in off the":

The fog came in off the bay, and the great trees were spreading and the stars were shining.

This is an architecture demo, not a strong language model. See the write-up for what worked, what didn't, and what's missing.

The v1.0 release has the exact checkpoint and data from the published run. After installing (step 1):

mkdir -p data runs/main curl -L -o runs/main/ckpt.pkl https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/deepseek-v3-jax/releases/download/v1.0/ckpt.pkl # 138 MB curl -L -o data/tokenizer.json https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/deepseek-v3-jax/releases/download/v1.0/tokenizer.json .venv/bin/python sample.py --prompt "The fog came in off the" --num 3

The checkpoint is a Python pickle, which can run code when loaded. Only load checkpoints from sources you trust.

You need an Apple Silicon Mac, Python 3.12 and uv. The published run used 24 GB of memory. No Mac? See Running on CPU.

1. Install

git clone https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/deepseek-v3-jax.git && cd deepseek-v3-jax uv venv -p 3.12 .venv uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python -r requirements.txt

Every version in requirements.txt is pinned. jax-metal 0.1.1 only works with jax==0.4.34, so don't upgrade JAX.

2. Check your setup

JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu .venv/bin/pytest tests.py -q # 39 passed .venv/bin/python smoke_metal.py # optional: what jax-metal supports on your Mac

In smoke_metal.py, "grad through 2-axis contraction" fails on jax-metal 0.1.1. That's expected, and the model is written to avoid it.

3. Build the dataset

.venv/bin/python prepare_data.py

This downloads the 207 books in sources.txt (~120 MB, about 7 minutes), cleans them, trains an 8,192-token BPE tokenizer and writes data/train.bin, data/val.bin and data/tokenizer.json. It should print:

train: 211 docs, 83.4M chars, 21.69M tokens val: 4 docs, 1.1M chars, 0.30M tokens

The published run's data had these hashes:

shasum -a 256 data/train.bin data/val.bin data/tokenizer.json d37aca97e707bb81b6e4d266cc1adfd1f3e3556457c6eb724e495118a734e0bb data/train.bin b7ac285b115e6793b5d36aa5b4bc6e81a5fccfc7af0908a306d3828ebca9c31c data/val.bin c5a142b4006a967c880dda44ad792719d53c16d947da3b6c2332d6132d9967cc data/tokenizer.json

You will most likely get different hashes. The Hammett books are pinned to exact Standard Ebooks commits and come out identical, but Project Gutenberg files can't be pinned, and Gutenberg has since re-issued 28 of the 203 books with small edits (mostly accents stripped, like "José" → "Jose"). The token counts come out the same, so training should behave the same.

To train on the exact same bytes, skip prepare_data.py and download the published data instead:

mkdir -p data for f in train.bin val.bin tokenizer.json; do curl -L -o data/$f https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/deepseek-v3-jax/releases/download/v1.0/$f; done shasum -a 256 data/*.bin data/tokenizer.json # should match the hashes above

4. Train

.venv/bin/python train.py # the main run: 12k steps, ~2.6 h .venv/bin/python train.py --steps 2000 --out runs/bias_on # balancing ablation, with the bias .venv/bin/python train.py --steps 2000 --out runs/bias_off --no-bias # ...and without it

Each run writes metrics.jsonl (loss, validation loss, per-expert load, biases, tokens/s) and ckpt.pkl (saved at every evaluation) into its --out folder, which defaults to runs/main. Seeds are fixed, but GPU math on Metal isn't bit-for-bit deterministic, so expect your numbers to land close to the ones above rather than match them exactly.

5. Generate

.venv/bin/python sample.py --prompt "The fog came in off the" --num 3

Defaults: temperature 0.8, top-k 50, 300 new tokens per sample (--temp, --top-k, --n).

6. Make the figures

.venv/bin/python plots.py # needs runs/main, runs/bias_on, runs/bias_off JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu .venv/bin/python charts.py # the rest of the write-up's charts

Both write into post/figures/.

To redraw the figures without training, download the logs from the release: metrics-main.jsonl, metrics-bias_on.jsonl and metrics-bias_off.jsonl go into runs/main/, runs/bias_on/ and runs/bias_off/ as metrics.jsonl. charts.py also needs the checkpoint and the data.

Everything runs without jax-metal. It's much slower, so use the smaller config:

JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu .venv/bin/python train.py --config small

--config small (4 layers, 8 experts, top-2, 128-token context) is meant for 8–16 GB Macs too. It has only been checked for a couple of steps, not trained to the end.

File What it is deepseek_v3.py The model: config, MLA, MoE, balancing, MTP, loss, train step, cached generation. The 190 lines. train.py Training loop: AdamW with warmup and cosine decay, evaluation, checkpoints, logging prepare_data.py, sources.txt Download, clean and tokenize the corpus sample.py Text generation from a checkpoint tests.py 39 tests: causal masking, cache vs full forward, routing, balancing, MTP targets, NaN handling, bf16 master weights, and more smoke_metal.py Which JAX operations work on Apple's GPU plots.py, charts.py The figures, all drawn from the logs, checkpoint and corpus post/ Diagrams, figures and screenshots from the write-up

"190 lines" counts the non-blank, non-comment lines of deepseek_v3.py after its docstring:

tail -n +5 deepseek_v3.py | grep -cvE '^\s*(#|$)' # 190 Dense MoE compute. Every expert runs on every token and the unpicked ones are zeroed. The routing math is exact, but there's no sparse dispatch or expert parallelism. No weight absorption in MLA. The latent is decompressed explicitly, which is easier to read and slower at inference. Not included: FP8 training, DualPipe, node-limited routing, YaRN context extension, and any post-training. Scale. 36.2M parameters vs 671B, 6 layers vs 61, a 256-token context vs 128K.

All training text is public domain in the United States: Dashiell Hammett's Red Harvest, The Dain Curse, The Maltese Falcon and Continental Op stories (CC0 editions from Standard Ebooks), plus about 200 detective and crime novels from Project Gutenberg. Every source is listed in sources.txt. Public-domain status outside the US may differ.

DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report, 2024.

Code: MIT. The training text is public domain in the US (see above).

item.title: PyPI's redesigned project pages with clearer security signals are now live
item.description:
PyPI's redesigned project pages with clearer security signals are now live

In July, we announced a series of planned updates to the PyPI user interface. Shaped by user research with members of the Python community, the updates aim to improve how we surface security signals and display package details.

We're pleased to share that this work is now complete and live on PyPI.

Context¶

With the rapid growth of the Python ecosystem, PyPI has become an increasingly attractive target for malicious actors. In response, the PyPI team has delivered many security features while taking a more active role in helping PyPI users assess and understand package security.

Digital attestations, introduced in 2024, are an example of this effort, providing a verifiable record of a release file's provenance (where it came from). However, provenance and attestations are still unfamiliar concepts for many PyPI users, and PyPI's interface did little to communicate their meaning, importance, or limitations.

To address this, PyPI partnered with Kabu Creative to bring clearer security signals to the PyPI UI, implementing the recommendations developed in the OpenSSF Attestations Style Guide.

Here's a look at what's changed, what it means for you, and what actions you can take.

The New Security Tab¶

The new security tab communicates release provenance states and displays per-file attestations, giving you a dedicated place to verify where the release files came from.

Provenance States¶

PyPI calculates each release's provenance state by checking whether each release file has an attestation. Typically, a release will be in one of two states:

Full Provenance¶

This means that 100% of the release files have attestations, carrying either or both of the supported attestation types:

PyPI Publish attestations confirm the file was published by a PyPI Trusted Publisher:

SLSA Build Provenance attestations link the file back to its exact source commit, build platform, and instructions:

You can review attestation metadata directly in the UI, or click on the transparency log link for more information.

No Provenance¶

"No provenance" simply means that no file in the release has an attestation. This is typical for older releases or projects that have not yet configured Trusted Publishing. No provenance does not necessarily indicate that a release or release file is malicious; it instead means that the file origin cannot be cryptographically verified.

When there is no provenance, you should rely on surrounding trust signals to assess security, such as maintainer history, release patterns, and repository activity. If you maintain the package, consider using Trusted Publishing with a publisher that generates attestations for your next release.

Provenance Warnings¶

Provenance warnings are designed to help you identify when a file may not have come from the project's maintainers, for example, if an attacker has taken over an account or a publishing workflow.

When provenance metadata looks unusual or conflicts with a project's history, PyPI surfaces a prominent warning. Many warnings have legitimate explanations, but each one is worth checking before you install.

Incomplete Provenance¶

This means that some files carry attestations while others do not (e.g., wheels were published via Trusted Publishing, but the source tarball was uploaded using an API token).

Exercise caution if you see this warning. Check release notes for build issues or ask in the project's issue tracker before installing.

Inconsistent Provenance¶

This warning indicates that files within the same release originate from different build systems or source repositories.

Check the attestation metadata to confirm whether all files came from sources controlled by the maintainers.

Change of Provenance¶

This warning tells you that the release files originated from a different repository or workflow than a previous release. While often legitimate (such as an organization name change or repository migration), it can also indicate a compromised pipeline or account takeover.

If you see this warning, check the project release notes or official channels to confirm that an infrastructure migration was planned.

Loss of Provenance¶

This means that a project that previously published with attestations has changed to uploading release files without them.

Check whether the maintainers intentionally changed their publishing process, for example by switching back to API tokens, or by changing their publishing configuration so that it no longer generates attestations. If this is unexpected, treat the release with skepticism until verified.

To learn more about provenance and attestations, including provenance warnings, see our user documentation.

Redesigned Project Detail Page¶

To support these changes, the project detail page has also been updated:

Provenance warnings now appear at the top of the page, alongside status banners for yanked releases, archived projects, and pre-releases. If a project or release is quarantined, only the quarantine banner is shown, as it takes precedence over all other warnings and banners. When a release has full provenance or provenance warnings, its provenance state is displayed in the sidebar, linking through to the security tab for more information. Metadata is now ordered by utility and labeled as "PyPI data" or "Data verified by PyPI", replacing the old design where data was grouped and ordered by verification status. Release Files and Release History¶

The redesigned release files tab helps you find the right file by searching and filtering long lists. You can also view the provenance state of each file within the table, and quickly identify late files, which are marked with an orange warning icon.

Late file warnings are shown when one or more files were uploaded more than 14 days after the initial release timestamp. These warnings only appear on releases prior to July 2026, when a policy was introduced to reject new files after 14 days.

The release history tab now also provides more details about each release, exposing file count, provenance state, and release status (i.e., quarantined, yanked, archived, or pre-release).

Getting Help¶

Alongside the interface updates, PyPI's user documentation has been extended to help you better navigate package security. Read our package security guide to learn about:

Looking Ahead & Acknowledgments¶

The new security tab gives PyPI a dedicated home for future attestation types and security notices. To help the wider open source ecosystem benefit from this work, we've also published a case study in the OpenSSF Attestations Style Guide detailing the design patterns and warnings developed during this project.

This initiative was funded by the Open Source Security Foundation and implemented by Kabu Creative. We would like to thank Dustin Ingram, Zach Steindler, and the members of the OpenSSF Securing Software Repositories Working Group for championing this effort. Special thanks to Mike Fiedler, Jacob Coffee, and members of the PyPI team for their thoughtful design feedback and code reviews, @cofiem for their contributions to the new release files tab, and our user interview participants and community testers for helping shape the final design.

Finally, we would like to thank the OpenSSF for its funding and continued partnership in securing the Python packaging ecosystem.

item.title: Lovable apps expose passport details and more than 200K private messages
item.description:
Lovable: Many Apps Built on the Platform Expose Sensitive Data

AI makes it easier to build your own web applications, but handling sensitive data still requires special care. We examined 159,041 Lovable projects and found many cases where personal and confidential information was accessible without logging in.

About Lovable

Lovable is a Swedish AI startup founded in Stockholm in 2023 by Anton Osika and Fabian Hedin. The platform turns plain-language descriptions into web applications and is designed to be accessible even to people with little or no programming experience.

Lovable grew out of Osika’s open-source project “GPT Engineer”, released in 2023. The project evolved into the GPT Engineer App before being renamed Lovable in late 2024 and launching publicly that November.

The Promise

Lovable can build impressively sophisticated web projects with AI, from static websites to full applications with user management and database connections. But as soon as an application handles confidential information, one question becomes crucial: Is that data protected against unauthorized access?

In its marketing, Lovable repeatedly emphasizes that no technical knowledge is needed to build projects. This can give the impression that the platform takes care of security too. Yet Lovable’s Terms & Conditions place responsibility for applications and data handling on the customers themselves.

That leaves a troubling gap between the promise of an easy-to-use, all-in-one service and the responsibilities customers are expected to take on.

Against this backdrop, we investigated how well sensitive data in Lovable applications is protected, in collaboration with Handelsblatt. Lina Knees reported on the findings on November 2, 2026 (in German).

Research Question

We wanted to find out whether sensitive data in Lovable applications was accessible without logging in. We looked separately at data sent when a website first loaded and additional content we checked by making further read-only requests with the same API key.

The result: We found many clear examples of sensitive data left unprotected.

Methodology

We focused on the database service Supabase. Its integration is relatively easy to analyze, and we believe it is the most widely used database service among Lovable projects. Lovable’s own database features, introduced in late 2025, are still less widely used. Similar misconfigurations may occur there too, but we did not examine them in this analysis.

Using datasets from the open web archive Common Crawl, we identified and analyzed 159,041 Lovable projects from December 2025 to September 2026. Of these, 34,545 used Supabase.

24,664 websites sent database records from Supabase as soon as they loaded, without requiring a login or any other interaction. That alone is not a security issue: the data may be intended for public display. But by making additional read-only requests, we were able to retrieve more database content. We found records containing email addresses in 10,560 tables across 7,403 of the 24,664 websites (30%).

Limitations

Email addresses can help identify records containing personal data, but they may also be public contact addresses or test data. At the same time, this approach misses personal records that contain no email address. These effects partly offset one another, though we could not establish to what extent. The 30% figure should therefore not be read as a confirmed data leak rate. It applies only to the 24,664 websites we examined more closely. Our sample, drawn from Common Crawl, is also not representative of all Lovable applications.

We retrieved only parts of the datasets rather than downloading them in full. The figures below reflect the records we actually downloaded; the affected datasets may contain more. We are not publishing details of how to access them, as doing so could make further access easier.

Data Leaks

We found many serious cases of exposed data, including:

A German lifestyle forum exposed more than 80,000 profiles containing full names, email addresses, dates of birth, and gender information. More than 200,000 chat messages were also accessible.

Several event organizers and restaurants exposed tens of thousands of records relating to ticket and food sales, with no login required. The records we inspected included email addresses, phone numbers, postal addresses, payment information, and ticket codes.

A property management company exposed AI-generated summaries of internal emails containing sensitive information about tenants, property owners, and business partners.

In a particularly serious case, a service provider exposed more than 1,000 records containing identity document details, including passport numbers, expiration dates, and nationalities. These highly sensitive identity details could be used for identity theft.

Other accessible content included tens of thousands of contracts, invoices, personal photo albums, and internal WhatsApp communications.

We also found numerous newsletter subscriptions, waiting lists, and contact and support inquiries. In one case, 280,000 emails sent to a provider’s customers were accessible.

Depending on what it contains, exposed data like this could be used for phishing, ticket fraud, or identity theft. We could not establish whether any of it had been misused.

Handelsblatt contacted Lovable with the findings of our investigation.

Implications

Our analysis shows that many Lovable applications leave even highly sensitive data unprotected, with potentially serious consequences for the people affected.

Access control mistakes can happen in any application, whether written by people or built with AI. With Lovable, database integrations follow recurring patterns, making it easier for attackers to look for similar misconfigurations across many applications. An approach that works against one app may then work against others with little extra effort. Users without a technical background also face a harder task spotting and preventing these flaws.

An easy-to-use development platform does not remove the need for an expert review of access permissions before an application handles confidential data.

Automated checks are no substitute for a professional security assessment.

Before an application handles real customer or business data, its access permissions, interfaces, and separation between user accounts should be reviewed. These checks should be repeated after significant changes. If the necessary expertise is not available in-house, bring in qualified support.

If you would like help securing your application, please get in touch.

Note: This research report presents a more recent analysis and updated figures compared with the Handelsblatt article published on November 2, 2026.

Get in touch for an informal conversation. We'll look at your current situation and work with you to find the right solutions.

item.title: A family tree of software job titles
item.description:
For a few years I was ‘Head of DevOps’. Before I got that job title I’d done much the same work under other names, and since then I’ve watched the same work get called SRE, and then it seemed to morph towards platform engineering. If you’ve been in this industry for any length of time you’ll have seen titles come and go like this, and you might have wondered where they all came from.

So I (with the help of Mr Claude) built this family tree of software job titles, from the 1940s to now.

It’s here: ianmiell.github.io/sw-job-title-family-tree

What It Is

There are 104 titles, from ‘Computer’ (a person, not a machine) at the top to ‘AI Agent / Context Engineer’ at the bottom.

Time runs from top to bottom, in five-year rows. The titles sit in seven coloured columns by family:

Development Analysis, architecture and leadership Operations and infrastructure Networks and security Data and AI Quality and test Support and customer-facing

A solid arrow means the title grew out of its parent. A dashed arrow means influence, or a common career move. Landmark titles are in bold.

On the site you can click a family to see just that column (here’s Data & AI), or click a title to get its history, background and connections (here’s SRE).

The whole thing is one Graphviz file and one JSON file of descriptions. Each title is one line in the .dot file, and the picture is rendered with:

$ dot -Tsvg job_title_family_tree.dot -o job_title_family_tree.svg

Adding a title is three small edits: a node in its family’s column, an entry in the row for its five-year period, and its parent arrows.

A word on the dates. They’re roughly when a title became common, not its first recorded use, and they’re my best estimates, not sourced citations. Some are well known (SRE at Google in 2003, ‘DevOps’ coined in 2009, ‘Data Scientist’ in 2008). Plenty are a ‘c.’ and a shrug.

Six Things I Noticed

Drawing it out made a few patterns hard to miss.

1) Coding Started Out as the Clerical Bit

In 1947, Goldstine and von Neumann’s ‘Planning and Coding of Problems’ split the work of using a computer in two: mathematicians planned the problem, and coders translated the plan into machine instructions. Coding was treated as lower-status clerical work, and much of it was done by women.

It turned out that coding eventually became the hard, creative part, and the coder merged into the programmer.

Go back further and it’s stranger still. Several of the first ENIAC programmers were recruited from the Army’s human computers, people whose job was to compute by hand. So the job gave its name to the machine, and its people to programming.

2) Titles Break Apart, Then Join Back Up

The webmaster turned up around 1993, and was often a single person who wrote the HTML, ran the webserver (often a box under a desk), answered the email, and kept the site up (sometimes by kicking it, more often by plugging it back in after kicking it).

By the mid-2000s the title had all but gone, as it was unfashionably ancient. The code went to web developers, the servers to sysadmins, and the content to editors and designers.

Then the web developer split into front-end and back-end around 2005, and the two joined back up again as ‘full-stack’ around 2008.

This is the centralisation/distribution see-saw I’ve written about before, playing out in job titles.

3) Some Titles Don’t Last

The prompt engineer made headlines in 2023 with a few eye-wateringly well-paid job listings. As the models got better, the skill became part of other jobs, and on the tree it gets absorbed into the AI engineer almost as soon as it appears.

The scrum master is a slower version of the same story: demand peaked in the 2010s, and many organisations have since folded it back into engineering management or delivery roles.

The newest title on the tree is the ‘AI Agent / Context Engineer’ (c. 2025). The description for it currently says “time will tell whether it stays a separate title”. I’m not taking bets.

4) Names Get Recycled

‘Systems Engineer’ is two different jobs on the tree. At IBM in the 1960s it was a pre-sales role, working with customers to design installations and get them running. In the 1990s, thanks largely to Microsoft’s MCSE certification, it meant a more senior, design-oriented sysadmin. Same title, different branch, no relation.

‘Configuration management’ started as a 1960s US defence discipline for tracking hardware changes, became software version control in the 1970s, and then came back decades later as the name for tools like Puppet and Chef.

5) The New Thing Is Often an Old Thing

The ‘forward deployed engineer’ (FDE) is one of the hottest titles of 2025, as OpenAI, Anthropic and plenty of AI startups hire FDEs to get AI working inside their customers’ organisations.

Palantir built its business around them from about 2010: software engineers embedded with a customer, often on site, building whatever is needed to make the product work for that customer’s problem.

Which sounds a lot like IBM’s systems engineers of the 1960s, who worked with customers before and after the sale, designing installations and getting systems running. (It also sounds a lot like old-style consulting, but I would say that.)

6) The DevOps Debate Is There

Ben Treynor Sloss defined SRE as “what happens when you ask a software engineer to design an operations team”. DevOps was meant as a culture of developers and operations working together, but by about 2011 ‘DevOps Engineer’ had become a job title, usually for whoever did the automation. On the tree, the arrow between SRE and DevOps points both ways. Platform engineering has both of them as parents, and was sold around 2022 as ‘the successor to DevOps’.

The Dev/Ops divide has never been resolved. It just keeps getting new names.

Why Bother?

When I’m asked what the difference is between a DevOps engineer, an SRE and a platform engineer, the honest answer is always a little history lesson. This is the shortest version of that lesson I’ve managed so far.

The dates are best guesses, and I’ll have missed titles, mangled some lineages and drawn arrows people will argue with. If you know better, let me know, or raise a PR on the repo.

Which brings me back to the coders.

In 1947 coding was the clerical bit, and the real work was in the planning. Wind forward eighty years and you’ll hear much the same said about coding again, because AI. Last time, the coders turned out to be doing the hard part.

I’ll leave you to draw that arrow yourself.

item.title: LinkedIn, Monster take down over 1000 fake job postings after CBC investigation
item.description:
Canada·CBC Investigates

LinkedIn, Monster take down over 1,000 fake job postings after CBC investigation Actual opportunity required monthly subscription and incentivized recruiting others

More than 1,500 misleading job postings — offering remote work, no experience needed — have been taken down from LinkedIn and Monster after a CBC visual investigation revealed the listings funnelled unsuspecting applicants to a multi-level marketing (MLM) company that asked for money.

CBC connected a network of travel-related pages posting suspicious jobs — positions like "Work From Home Travel Planner and Virtual Customer Support Representative" — to a U.S.-based MLM called Evolution Travel. Some of the roles promised to pay up to $75,000 US per year.

In reality, there was no job and no salary.

Applicants were quickly directed to join virtual information sessions, where they were asked to pay hundreds of dollars up front, followed by a monthly subscription fee. The program promised to teach members how to make money from booking travel as an independent agent and recruiting others into the program, taking a cut of their commissions.

The companies went by names like Wanderwell Collective, Professional Travel Hub, Remote-Careers, Sky Land & Ocean Travel and Sunkissed Getaways.

The job postings made no mention of Evolution Travel or sign-up fees.

Many of the jobs did not require experience and promised to pay up to $75,000 US. (Illustration: Matthew Hoddy/CBC; LinkedIn)

"This is disgusting," said Jay Jones, a Chicago-based job listing investigator who CBC shared its findings with. "They catch you with the lure of the fake job. The money is great, [successful applicants] get to stay at home. You have to pay to get work — that's not how work works."

Misleading job postings — including ones that require payment or lead to MLMs — are strictly prohibited on platforms like LinkedIn and other job sites.

Jay Jones investigates misleading and fake jobs online. (CBC)

"It feels in so many ways that we're living in a funhouse mirror," said Vass Bednar, managing director of the Canadian Shield Institute, a public policy think-tank that focuses on economic resilience and digital sovereignty.

These postings risk "eroding confidence — confidence in the self and confidence that there is, frankly, meaningful work out there for people that is worth pursuing."

Jobs were 'misleading': LinkedIn

MLMs are not illegal in Canada or the U.S. However, in the U.S., companies and individuals could face fines if they are found to violate the U.S. Federal Trade Commission Act, which prohibits "unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce."

"I would consider [these job posts] misleading… and would invite enforcement by either the FTC, the state governments or other federal enforcement agencies," said William Kovacic, former FTC chairman and commissioner, with whom CBC also shared its findings.

One independent agent behind multiple travel businesses linked to misleading jobs ads CBC identified — Wanderwell Collective, Destination Knot, Aisle and Abroad, and Professional Travel Hub — was Diedre Norton. In one video posted to YouTube, Norton said she had a network of 300 recruits for Evolution Travel.

Even though Evolution Travel’s founder, David McCovy, praised her in online videos as being a top performer, Norton denied being affiliated with the program before hanging up on CBC News.

Screenshot of an online video showing Evolution founder David McCovy during a conference. (EvolutionTravelCafe/YouTube)

McCovy did not respond to CBC’s requests for comment.

A representative from Evolution Travel who only identified themselves by their title, chief operating officer, told CBC they have consistently told their independent agents not to post job ads on any platforms.

Late last month, LinkedIn took down close to 900 ads connected to Evolution Travel, saying it had removed them because they were "misleading and violated" company policy, adding "the companies behind them will no longer be able to post jobs" on the platform.

Monster took down 600 listings, saying it has "clear policies prohibiting misleading job postings and multi-level marketing opportunities, and we take action to remove listings that do not meet our standards."

Hundreds of job postings posted to LinkedIn and Monster actually brought applicants into the recruiting process for a multi-level marketing company, a CBC News visual investigation has found. (Illustration: Matthew Hoddy/CBC, LinkedIn, Monster)

Detecting fake jobs

Evolution Travel does not operate in Canada, but CBC journalists still came across the job posting in their feeds. They were also recommended in emails from LinkedIn.

The ads contained immediate red flags. The travel companies named in the ads had minimal to no presence online, and there were close to 1,500 postings, often with almost identical job descriptions.

Many of the jobs did not require experience and were remote. CBC found more than 1,500 misleading or fake jobs. (LinkedIn)

The jobs, in many cases, required no education, no prior experience and often did not require a resumé.

CBC applied for eight jobs on LinkedIn and Monster, attaching a blank document as a resumé in cases that required it. Upon applying, the team was sent automated emails to join a virtual information session by individuals connected to Evolution Travel.

CBC journalists were sent automated emails and asked to join a virtual information session by individuals connected to Evolution Travel upon applying for the jobs. (CBC)

Evolution Travel and its partner Archer Travel Services describe themselves as an international "home-based travel business" that trains its members to book travel and earn a commission.

But it's not just about booking travel. Archer Travel’s website describes Evolution Travel as its "recruiting partner" and describes it as a "network marketing" company — another term for multi-level marketing, according to the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

A compensation plan for members on Evolution Travel’s website shows a percentage of commissions and monthly bonuses are paid to the most effective recruiters, with membership tiers up to "8 Star Platinum" for recruiting 100,000 people.

Documents show compensation plans for Evolution Travel. (Evolution Travel)

None of this was mentioned in the information sessions CBC attended, which covered travel booking exclusively. When a CBC journalist posing as a job applicant asked about getting commissions from their own recruits, the session host said it was not covered in the information sessions and that the person who invited them into the program would address it.

Session hosts also didn’t disclose there is a hidden $50 annual fee in the independent contractor agreement, seen by CBC, when signing up.

A screenshot from an Evolution virtual session shows the packages attendees can pay to enrol in the program. (Evolution Travel)

Former FTC chairman and commissioner Kovacic said if he were still at the agency, he would be looking into the company.

"[Fees are] not presented in the initial interaction," he said. "It's shrouded in a way that's very important and would mislead users."

27,000 independent contractors

Job seekers have been complaining about Evolution Travel, its members and agents like Deidre Norton online and to the Better Business Bureau for years.

In 2021, Evolution Travel was among 1,000 companies put on notice by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission that they could face fines if they or their representatives made "misleading, or deceptive representations" about a "money-making opportunity."

Kovacic said a firm that "defied" FTC notices and continued to persist in these practices would be a "worthy target for an investigation."

CBC News found numerous complaints online about companies linked to the job postings. (Illustration: Matthew Hoddy/CBC, Reddit, Better Business Bureau)

Ron Archer, the CEO of Archer Travel Services, said that the company does "not condone illegal job postings and addresses them when we are made aware."

Yet in videos online, travel agents connected to Evolution Travel talked openly about using LinkedIn job postings to recruit people into the business.

Archer said they cannot "tell people how they train for their business" because they have "27,000 independent contractors around the world."

"LinkedIn is a big one," said one member in a June 2026 training video posted to YouTube. "We have quite a few different trainings on how to post on LinkedIn."

Jay Jones, who has gotten tens of thousands of jobs taken down from platforms himself, said companies like LinkedIn and Monster generate revenue through this traffic.

"There's no actual vetting of what companies get to be created, what jobs get to be listed," said Jones. "People coming [to LinkedIn] believing that there are real opportunities are greeted with this MLM nonsense."

item.title: Dartmouth (Guarini) will not admit math PhD cohort this year
item.description:
The Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies has suspended admissions to the next cohort in its math Ph.D. program, which would matriculate in the 2027-2028 academic year. Guarini dean Carrie Colla ’01 and College spokesperson Jana Barnello did not specify when or whether the program would resume admissions.

Colla wrote in a Nov. 10 email statement to The Dartmouth that Guarini “regularly considers how to best invest in graduate education.”

“As part of those regular reviews, we are pausing admissions to the math Ph.D. program for the 2027-2028 cycle while the School of Arts and Sciences conducts a department review,” she wrote.

The decision to suspend the program “was made in close partnership with leaders in the School of Arts and Sciences and we look forward to working collaboratively with the department on this review,” Colla added.

She wrote in a Nov. 10 email to current graduate students that there “will be opportunities for students to participate in the review” and that she would meet with math graduate students and department faculty on Nov. 17. Graduate students can also reach out to math department chair Dimitrios Giannakis and math professor Vladimir Chernov to share questions and concerns, she wrote.

“While I know it is disappointing news that your cohort will not be growing next year, I am confident that this approach will allow us to strengthen the experience of both our Ph.D. students and the undergraduate students in the department,” Colla wrote.

During a Q&A at the Nov. 9 general faculty meeting, which The Dartmouth attended but was not permitted to record, faculty raised concerns about the suspension. Math professor Peter Winkler, who opposed the suspension, said at the meeting the decision was communicated to math department faculty on Nov. 6. Winkler declined to provide additional comment after the meeting.

The Ph.D. program’s pause follows a national trend of decreasing Ph.D. program seats. Data collected from 55 undisclosed research institutions demonstrated that Ph.D. acceptances dropped 15% in 2026 from the previous year, even though domestic applications increased.

In a Nov. 10 email to current graduate students, which was obtained and reviewed by The Dartmouth, Giannakis wrote that faculty members were “continuing to engage” with College administrators to “find a path forward” that would “eventually resume” the Ph.D. program.

Giannakis added in the email that Colla and School of Arts and Sciences dean Nina Pavcnik would attend a math department faculty meeting on Nov. 11 to discuss the suspension. “While I do not expect a reversal of the decision to pause admissions, I hope there will at least be a constructive dialogue with actionable outcomes,” he wrote.

Giannakis was unable to comment by time of publication.

The Guarini admissions office communicated the decision to applicants on Nov. 10, according to an email obtained by The Dartmouth. Any materials or recommendation letters that have already been submitted “will not be reviewed,” the Guarini admissions office wrote. Applications for the program, which typically accepts seven to nine students per year, would have been due on Dec. 15, 2026, according to the math department website.

“We recognize this is disappointing news and we are sorry for the disruption to your plans,” the email to people who already submitted application materials reads. On Nov. 10, Colla wrote to current math graduate students that “status and support” for current students “are not changing” and that the program will see “every currently enrolled student through graduation,” according to an email obtained and reviewed by The Dartmouth.

“Stipends, insurance and the five-year funding guarantee all remain in place for students making satisfactory academic progress,” Colla wrote. “Advising relationships, qualifying exams, degree requirements and teaching and research appointments will continue as planned.”

Guarini Ph.D. students received an annual stipend of $49,862.40 for the 2026-2027 academic year, along with tuition remission, health insurance and other benefits, according to the Guarini website. The College guarantees five years of financial support to students making satisfactory academic progress. Graduate students typically teach “one course in each of their final three years of study,” according to the math department graduate student handbook. Starting this term, math Ph.D. candidates must also serve as a teaching assistant for one term each year after their third year, while first and second-year Ph.D. candidates must serve as teaching assistants for three terms a year instead of the previously required two, according to the handbook.

Third-year math Ph.D. candidate Jacob Lehmann Duke GR said he and his fellow graduate students learned of the suspension from Colla’s Nov. 10 email. He said he was “frustrated” by the “lack of transparency” surrounding the decision. “We were all shocked,” he said. “There was no indication that this was coming.”

Second-year math Ph.D. candidate Alex Moon GR said they believe suspending applications for the upcoming cycle sends “a message of instability” to future applicants.

“Part of the deal of graduate school is that you want there to be minimal factors outside of your control that will prevent you from getting this Ph.D.,” Moon said. “If this is something they do once, it’s something they can do later.”

In an interview with The Dartmouth, second-year math Ph.D. candidate Aidan Hennessey GR said “losing out on a cohort of students” would negatively affect the discussions among the “already quite small” Ph.D. program.

“Having people in adjacent areas of math to you — that you can talk about math and learn from, teach and talk through ideas with — all of this is very helpful,” Hennessey said. “Having more students around is nice for community.”

Lehmann Duke added that the suspension could put undergraduates intending to enroll in graduate-level mathematics courses “at a real deficit.”

Ben Singer ’27 — who said they have taken graduate-level math courses since their freshman year — added that there are “a few core graduate courses” that are “really important for undergraduates here who want to get into graduate school.” A decrease in Ph.D. students raises questions about whether those classes will be offered, whether undergraduates will be able to take them and how fewer course offerings will affect people who want to go to graduate school, Singer said.

The College “reserves the right to make changes in the offering” or cancel a course with fewer than five enrolled students, according to the Arts and Sciences Registrar’s Office website.

First-year computational science and modeling Ph.D. candidate Ethan Baird GR said “almost half” of his program’s coursework requirements are typically fulfilled through mathematics department courses. Baird added that these classes are the “basis of everything that we end up doing later,” which leads him to worry that the suspension of the admissions will have trickle-down effects on the computational science and modeling Ph.D. programs. Math major Ribhu Hooja ’27 said the department “did not officially” inform undergraduate students about the pause and that he instead found out from graduate students. If the pause lasts “even for a year, there could still be harm” because of “the relationships formed” between undergraduate and graduate students in advanced math classes, Hooja said.

“We learn how to apply to grad school, and what it means,” Hooja said. “It’s an important relationship I’ve really benefitted a lot from.”

Third-year Ph.D. candidate Michaela Polley GR said she was concerned about the pause’s effects on “research culture” among Dartmouth graduates and undergraduates alike.

“The idea of being a research university and a liberal arts college doesn’t work if you don’t have graduate students,” she said.

During the Nov. 9 meeting, College President Sian Leah Beilock and Pavcnik also addressed faculty concerns about the College’s discontinuation of the Society of Fellows, a three-year interdisciplinary research program established in 2014 to support postdoctoral research and scholarship. The Society has stopped recruiting new fellows and will conclude in summer 2028, when its current cohort completes their appointments, according to the program’s website. Beilock said at the meeting that the decision follows the need to reinvest funding in other institutional priorities.

Beilock announced at the meeting that the College is “working to reduce Dartmouth’s spending by $50 million,” in order to increase faculty and staff salaries “especially if and when inflation continues to rise,” according to a transcript of her speech published on the Office of the President’s website.

In a Nov. 11 email statement to The Dartmouth, Barnello wrote that the $50 million “reflects adjustments already made” to the budget, and that “roughly half” is “already in place” for fiscal year 2027.

Beilock also announced at the meeting that the College is “preparing” to convert North Park apartments, which are currently listed on the Office of Residential Life website as undergraduate housing, to graduate student housing. The North Park apartments have exclusively housed undergraduates since the 2022-2023 academic year, according to the Dartmouth Graduate Student Council website.

Correction appended (Nov. 12, 9:30 a.m.): A previous version of this article referred to Alex Moon as he. They use they/them pronouns.

Sahil Gandhi ’29 is a reporter from Staten Island, N.Y., and is majoring in environmental studies and government modified with philosophy and economics. He loves word searches and falling down internet and Wikipedia rabbit holes. He can be reached at sgandhi@thedartmouth.com.
